why: The palindrome (i, j) DP on the concatenation word1 + word2, with one twist in what you read from the table: only an outermost matched pair with i in word1 and j in word2 guarantees both words contribute.
hints: Any chosen subsequences concatenated form a subsequence of word1 + word2. So start from the longest palindromic subsequence of the concatenation.
The danger is a palindrome taken from one word only. Its outermost pair decides it: if the outer s[i] == s[j] has i in word1 and j in word2, both words are used.
Run dp[i][j] = LPS of s[i..j] on s = word1 + word2, and take the maximum of dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 over pairs with s[i] == s[j], i < len(word1) <= j. O((n+m)^2).
pitfalls: Returning plain LPS of the concatenation fails example 2 ('abcdef' would give 1).
The inside of the palindrome may come entirely from one word; only the outer pair must straddle.
